# 2 Maccabees Chapter 2 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 2 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_002_page_001.jpg

---

**1** The same records also tell us that Jeremiah the prophet commanded those about to be taken into exile to bring along some of the sacred fire — as we mentioned earlier.

**2** He also gave them a copy of the law and urged the exiles: do not let the commandments of the LORD slip from your minds. Do not be dazzled by the gold and silver idols you will see there, or seduced by their splendor.

**3** He kept pressing on them, with many more words like these, that the law must never leave their hearts.

**4** The same document also records that, acting on a divine revelation, the prophet ordered that the Tent of Meeting and the ark of the covenant should be carried with him when he departed to the mountain that Moses had climbed — the mountain where Moses had looked out over the land God was giving his people.

**5** When Jeremiah arrived, he discovered a cave there. He carried the Tent of Meeting inside, along with the ark and the altar of incense, then he sealed the entrance shut.

**6** Some of those who had followed tried to memorize the path so they could find it again — but they never could.

**7** When Jeremiah found out, he confronted them and said: "The place will remain hidden until the day God gathers his people together once more and shows them his mercy.

**8** Then the LORD will bring all of this to light. The glory of the LORD will appear — the cloud will be seen again — just as it was shown to Moses, and just as Solomon prayed for when he asked that the place be truly consecrated."

**9** It is also clear from these records that this same Solomon, in his wisdom, offered a sacrifice at the dedication and completion of the temple.

**10** When Moses prayed to the LORD, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offerings. In the same way, when Solomon prayed, fire came down and consumed his offerings too.

**11** Moses himself had explained it: "Because the sin offering was not eaten, it was consumed instead."

**12** Solomon likewise observed eight days of celebration.

**13** These same events are also recorded in the memoirs of Nehemiah — how he established a library and collected the writings about the kings and the prophets, the psalms of David, and the letters of foreign kings about their gifts to the temple.

**14** Judas Maccabeus did the same kind of work: he gathered up all the books that had been scattered and lost during the war, and they are now safely in our hands.

**15** If you need any of them, send someone to fetch them.

**16** Since we are preparing to celebrate the festival of the temple's purification, we are writing to let you know. Please join in observing these days.

**17** It is God who has saved his whole people. He has given to all of us the heritage, the kingdom, the priesthood, and the holy consecration —

**18** just as he promised in the law. And we trust that God will soon have mercy on us and gather us from every corner of the earth back to the holy place; for he has already rescued us from great disasters and cleansed the sanctuary.

**19** What follows is the story of Judas Maccabeus and his brothers: the cleansing of the great temple, the rededication of the altar,

**20** and the campaigns against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator —

**21** and the miraculous interventions from heaven granted to those who fought with passion for their faith. Though their numbers were small, they ransacked the entire land of the enemy, routed those barbarian hordes,

**22** won back the temple known to the whole world, liberated the city, and saved the laws that were on the verge of being wiped out — all because the LORD in his great kindness had compassion on them.

**23** All of this was laid out by Jason of Cyrene across five volumes. We are now going to try to compress it all into a single book.

**24** When we look at the sheer volume of material and the difficulty it presents to anyone who wants to engage seriously with this history —

**25** we have aimed to make something that is enjoyable to read, accessible to those who want to memorize it, and useful to every reader.

**26** For those of us doing the work of condensing — it has not been easy. It has required real effort and many sleepless nights.

**27** Think of someone throwing a dinner party who wants every guest to enjoy themselves. It is hard work — but to earn the gratitude of many people, we will take it on gladly.

**28** We will leave the precise details to the original historian. Our job is simply to follow the rules of a good summary.

**29** An architect overseeing new construction must think about every part of the whole building. But the artist brought in to paint decorative murals only has to think about what is beautiful in its context. We are in the position of the muralist.

**30** Investigating every angle, ranging across the entire subject — that is the work of the original historian.

**31** The epitomist, on the other hand, should be free to aim for conciseness, and not be expected to say everything.

**32** So let our narrative begin here. Enough of the preamble — it would be absurd to write a long introduction and then turn around and cut the history short.
